"""The record's tool: it owns the form of FACTS.md and POSITIONS.md and of
their two history files, and is the only way to write them.

An entry is one line under a permanent number, `- F-87 **Title.** Text.` in
explorations/coordinator/FACTS.md and `- P-48 **Title.** Text.` in
POSITIONS.md. A number is never reused or changed: a new entry takes the
highest number its file has ever used, plus one. An entry stands under the
nearest `## ` or `### ` heading above it, its section. Its title is its bold
opening, or where it has none, its opening words up to the first colon,
semicolon or full stop.

A pointer is another entry's number in the sentence that needs it, alone
(`It builds P-48.`) or with the first words of the target's title in quotes
(`It builds P-48, "A type parameter the arguments do not fix ..."`, or
`P-48 ("...")`). Quoted words must open the target's current title (`...` or
`…` marks words left out); when an entry is retitled, the tool rewrites them
in every entry that points to it, in the same call.

The history (FACTS-history.md, POSITIONS-history.md beside the record) holds,
under `### F-87`, one block per change, oldest first: one provenance line (the
UTC time from the clock, the kind of change, `from` each report section,
`commit`, `by`, then the note after a colon), and the line as it stood before
the change. The tool derives the kind: `added`, `rewritten`, `moved to "S"`,
`merged into F-n`, `F-n merged in`, `removed`; the numbering wrote one
`numbered` block per entry. A retitle that refreshed other entries' pointer
words, or a merge that moved their pointers, says so in one more line of the
block (`pointer words refreshed in: F-12, P-48`).

Every write takes a lock (flock on .record.lock beside the record), checks the
state it would leave, appends the history blocks first and then replaces each
record file in one step. A write is refused only for what would break the
store: a bad number, a pointer that does not resolve or whose words do not
open its target's title, a line break in an entry, no provenance (neither
`--from` nor `--note`). Never for size. The tool does not commit: commit the
record file and its history together.

usage: record.py COMMAND [ARGS] [PROVENANCE] [--root DIR]

  PROVENANCE: --from PATH#HEADING (repeatable; PATH from the repository root
  or from explorations/, HEADING held by exactly one heading of it, as doc:
  resolves one), --commit HASH (in HEAD's history), --by WHO, --note WHY.
  Each write needs --from or --note.

  add F|P --section TITLE FILE   a new entry from FILE's one line, numbered
      record.py add F --section 'Landed semantics' new.md --from 'compile-ladder/rung-x/REPORT.md#The fix' --by coordinator
  set N [FILE] [--section TITLE] entry N rewritten from FILE's line, or moved
      record.py set F-87 f87.md --from 'compile-ladder/rung-x/REPORT.md#The question' --note 'cut to the form'
  merge N --into M [FILE]        N removed, M rewritten from FILE (or kept),
                                 every pointer to N made a pointer to M
      record.py merge F-90 --into F-87 f87.md --note 'one fact, two entries'
  remove N                       N removed; refused while a pointer to it remains
      record.py remove P-131 --note 'evicted to the coordinator skill, references/briefing.md'
  apply FILE                     many changes from one file, all or none (below)
      record.py apply chunk3.md --by 'consolidation chunk 3'
  check [--base COMMIT]          the store's checks; exit 1 on a failure
      record.py check --base cc9424c2a

# Climb batch 18

## 1. For the curator

### The words this record uses

- **Walk** is the interpreter. It runs a program without static types. The **compiled path** checks a program's types with the **checker**, then makes JVM bytecode.
- **The one library** is the interpreter's library (`Library/`, `ProjectFortress/LibraryBuiltin/`). At the **switch-over** the compiled path takes it over.
- **The distance** is the number of errors the checker reports on the one library. Each error has a **site** (a file and a line). **The count** is the checker's errors on the library's `FortressLibrary` component, read by the **count stage**, which also gives the checker's time.
- A **row** is an entry of the gap ledger, cited by number. An **item** is a numbered question in PLAN's list "Pavol's answers".
- A **rung** is one fix, built by one worker in its own copy of the tree and checked by a second worker, the skeptic. A **batch** is a few rungs, merged and tested together by the **gate** and landed at once. **The gather** lands the approved rungs on `main` one by one; a new row is written `NEW-X-1` and the like until the gather numbers it.
- **Test first.** Every fix starts with a test that shows the defect, seen failing before the edit and passing after. An **expected failure** is a test named `XXX...` that passes while the defect is there; when the fix lands it is **promoted** to a plain name.
- A **generic dotted method** is a method with static parameters of its own, called as `x.f(...)`. Its **bounds** are the types its static parameters must extend; its **coercion targets** are the types an argument may be converted into.
- **Way A** is the row 766 probe's fix: walk reads such a method's bounds and coercion targets in the trait's **method environment**, where the method's instances already read their parameter types, instead of the trait's **member environment**, which has no parent.
- **Conditional extension** is an `extends` entry with a `where` clause of constraints, as `List[\E\] extends LexicographicOrder[\List[\E\],E\] where { E extends StandardTotalOrder[\E\] }`: a list is ordered exactly when its elements are. **B.3** is the where-clause probe's shadow of it in the checker.
- **P-148**, your rule of 14 October: a rung that changes the checker times the count stage before and after its change, then makes a second pass that makes the checker faster without changing what it accepts, refuses or says.

### Where the distance stands

- After climb batch 17 the distance is 35 and the count 31, the count stage 76 s and the distance stage 180 s ([gate](https://github.com/palimondo/fortress/blob/main/explorations/compile-ladder/climb-batch-17/gate/distance.txt); F-53, F-240).
- What the batch moves: rung X, 1 site, `FortressLibrary.fss:2063`, `LexicographicOrder`'s `a CMP b` (class G1, row 634's list half), by the probe's measurement on its own base (37 to 36, nothing new) and by reading on this one; rung K none by reading; rung W changes walk only and moves nothing.
- **The distance expected after the batch: 34, by reading. The count: 30, by reading**, since `:2063` is a typecheck error of the `FortressLibrary` component, which the count holds. Neither is declared. Both are reported, never red (P-39).

### The batch: three rungs

- **W, walk reads a trait's generic method's bounds where the trait declares them (rows 766 and 765), and walk's load check names the rule that refuses a generic pair.** Today a generic dotted method that a trait declares gets quietly wrong instances under walk: `Maker.wrap(z, w)` on a `ZZ32` and a `ZZ64` gives `Box[\AnyIntegral\]` with the `ZZ32` not converted, and `Maker.make()` gives `Empty[\BOTTOM\]`, against P-46, P-48 and P-74. Way A is built and measured: +27 -4 lines in two walk files, both expected failures red on the base and green on it, `testSystem` 649 tests with no failure ([probe](https://github.com/palimondo/fortress/blob/main/explorations/perf-probes/trait-generic-method-inference/REPORT.md)). Beside it, walk's refusal of a generic pair still says "at least one pair of parameters must have excluding types", the rule P-45 removed; the message names the rule that failed, and the tests keyed on the old message are rekeyed (the landing review, finding 3).
- **X, conditional extension in the checker, for the list comparisons' site (row 634's list half).** P-151's last form: a trait that extends another under a `where` condition is that type only where it holds, and its members are checked with it holding. Built as the probe's shadow B.3, re-based onto climb batch 17's rungs A and L; `LexicographicOrder`'s element bounded by `StandardTotalOrder`, `List`'s entry under the condition, and a structural `=` kept on `List` so that a list of pairs keeps its equality ([where-clauses probe](https://github.com/palimondo/fortress/blob/main/explorations/perf-probes/where-clauses/REPORT.md), B.3; [tuple-comparisons judgement](https://github.com/palimondo/fortress/blob/main/explorations/reviews/tuple-comparisons-judgement.md), sections 2 and 3). The site goes, 35 to 34.
- **K, the `where` conditions checked where they apply (rows 748, 749, 750, 753 and 771).** A method's condition on its trait's parameter at a dotted call; a constraint whose bound names a `where`-clause variable, by inferring the variable; a trait's own constraint where its type is used; and a type `where`-clause variable bounded by its binding in the extender check (row 753) and by the clause's constraint at its opening (row 771). Row 771's own note says it waits on row 753, so 753 comes with it. Not probed; each traced to its lines.
- **Why two checker rungs, not one.** Conditional extension with rows 748, 749, 750 and 771, and 753 beside 771, would change seven checker files and five library files in one rung, of which only conditional extension has a shadow; batch 17's workers wrote 0.41M to 0.52M each, its biggest a re-based shadow (A, 0.52M). Split, each rung is the size of one of those, and the two share no declaration (section 3, "The rule the rungs keep").
- If the run must be shorter, K goes first, from its last rows back; W and X stay.

### What the batch leaves out (section 4)

- **Row 697 and P-152's probe**, PLAN's next two items after conditional extension: the coordinator's scope puts them after this batch. Row 697 is read against rung L's landed library first, and the probe starts from rung G's code.
- **Members scoped to the condition** (the coordinator's call on the peers' way, listed for you): it needs rung K's check of a condition at a dotted call, so it waits for the batch after, as a new row. **Walk's half of conditional extension** (walk reads the extension at every instance) waits too, as a new row with an expected-failure test. **The code generator's half** is row 701, after the switch-over.
- PLAN item 16's other candidates, each with what it waits on (section 4).

### Before the batch runs

- **Two questions for you, each with its default** (section 2): item 60, row 766's way (default A); and whether a list of floats gets a partial order under conditional extension (default no). Neither holds the batch: each default can be undone, and none reverses a decision of yours.
- The coordinator first makes the pending script edit (the gather's order, `coordinator/pending-script-edit.md`, its last section; done at `ac74e11c4`), then splices `plan-18/manifest/`, builds the base build, and keeps `/home/user/fortress-probe-where` until the batch lands, since rung X reads its diff.

### Cost

- About 4.0M tokens written, from 3.6M if no fix is contested to 4.7M with a judge and a repair round; a red gate adds about 0.5M. Batch 17 wrote 6.52M for five rungs, 1.30M a rung (`reviews/batch-17-review.md`, section 5).
  - Workers about 1.5M: X 0.55M (a shadow to re-base, five library files, the specification's box and entry, the stages), K 0.55M (five rows by reading in five files, the stages), W 0.40M (a patch that exists, a message, eight test files).
  - Skeptics about 1.3M; the fixed roles about 1.2M.
- About 5 hours at two agents at once (batch 17: 5 h 28 min for five rungs).

## 2. Your answers this batch takes, and the coordinator's calls it builds

### Two questions for you, one per item, each with its default

1. **Item 60, row 766: which way walk repairs a trait's generic dotted method.** Way A reads the method's bounds and coercion targets in the trait's method environment, where its instances already read their types (`way-a.patch`); every trait value then equals the same method's in an object and as a function, and the compiled values do not move (the probe, section 5). Way D gives every trait method that environment, which reaches the overload comparisons and member lookup, and the team kept the two apart ("not yet, it changes overloading semantics", `GenericMethod.java:91-92`). Way C restores the base's loud refusal, which keeps P-48 by stopping and gives none of the checker's values. **Default: A**, rung W. It reverses nothing: P-46, P-48 and P-74 ask for these values.
2. **A list of floats: ordered or not under conditional extension.** The rung bounds `LexicographicOrder`'s element by `StandardTotalOrder`, as the judgement's bound and the team's advanced library do (`Library/incomplete/advanced/Fortress.PartialTotalOrders.fss:117-140`), so the checker gives no order to a list of `RR64`, `QQ` or `Range` values, which are partially ordered; the text says such a list is "partial or total depending on whether the ordering of the elements is partial or total" (`Specification/advanced-lib/algebraic-constraints.tex:519-522`). A second entry under `StandardPartialOrder` would need a lexicographic partial order that the team did not write. Walk keeps today's behaviour for such lists until walk's half lands. **Default: one entry, no order for such a list on the checker**, by P-151's "add nothing it did not", stated in Appendix I's new entry. It can be undone: the other way adds an entry and its trait later.

### The coordinator's calls this batch builds, listed for your review

Each is settled by the record's principles and is reversible; none reverses a decision of yours, so none holds the batch.

1. **Way A's two measured lines kept as the probe left them.** The bound read at `EvaluatorBase.java:491` is kept, since a bound that names another static parameter needs it; `inferByUnification` at `:875` is left, since reading the bound there moved no value and turned one refusal into the function path's internal error (the probe, section 4).
2. **The message names the rule by the specification's name**, as the checker names its own: the No Duplicates Rule keeps walk's message for equal domains, "fails because their parameter lists have the same types"; the Return Type Rule and the Meet Rule each get theirs. Six tests key on the old message, not two: `GenericReturnRuleInvariantWalk` and `GenericReturnRuleOuterParamWalk`, which the review names because they pass on any refusal, and `NoDuplicatesRuleWalk`, `NoDuplicatesRuleSizeWalk`, `GenericOverloadInstancesApartWalk` and `GenericBoundsNoMeetWalk`. Each is rekeyed to the rule its own comment names.
3. **Conditional extension split from the four rows**, for its size, and row 753 added to rung K, since row 771's note says it waits on 753.
4. **Members checked under the condition, as P-151 says, and not yet scoped to it.** A member so checked stays callable where the condition fails, the probe's hole. Scoping it needs a dotted call's check of a condition on the trait's parameter, which rung K builds as row 748, so it waits for the batch after; rung X files it as NEW-X-1. The team's own note foresaw it: "With conditional subtyping (or conditional methods), we may also not be able to tell whether a trait has a particular method" (`Specification/appendices/internal-document.tex`, its subsection "No Wrapped Fields Whose Types Are Naked Type Variables").
5. **Walk's half waits.** Walk reads an extension under a `where` clause as holding at every instance, and checks an override under it since climb batch 13 (`e8d377669`). Rung X files the reading as NEW-X-2 with an expected-failure walk test. Building it would change walk's values: a list of tuples or of floats would lose its `<` under walk.
6. **A structural `=` on `List`, outside the condition**, with `LexicographicOrder`'s body, as the judgement asks: without it a list of pairs, not ordered, falls to the identity `=` on the checker (`NumberOrderListDeclarations.fss:48` compares such lists).
7. **Only an `extends` clause of constraints alone is conditional**; a clause that binds a new variable keeps today's reading (the probe's B.6), and Appendix I's "Where-clause variables in extends clauses" bars such a variable from an `extends` clause.
8. **The team's comment "a hack to avoid the error of overloaded methods"** (`FortressLibrary.fss:3232`), now above the team's real generic `distribute`, is removed by rung X, the next library rung, as PLAN's default for the review's finding 7 says.
9. **Row 749's repair makes the checker refuse a call that the team's walk test runs**: `GenericFnWithExcludes.fss:44`, `g(O, P)` with `P` a `Y[\2\]`, which no `n` meets, refused by the text. The test runs under walk only, so its verdict stays; the point is listed.

### Points the batch lists for you, not questions

- **Team lines changed:** walk's inference of a trait's generic method and its load check's messages (W); `LexicographicOrder`'s static parameters, `List`'s and `PureList`'s `extends` lines, the comment at `:3232`, and the checker's subtype case of a trait type, its trait and object declaration checks (X); the checker's dotted call, its arrow of a declaration, its trait-type check and its extender check (K).
- **What walk does differently:** a trait's generic dotted method takes the instance its object's own method takes, the `ZZ32` converted, its bound where nothing fixes it (W); an inherited generic functional method beside a plain one is chosen where only it fits (W, row 765); a refused generic pair names its rule (W). The library change moves no walk value (X).
- **What the checker does differently:** a list is ordered only where its elements are totally ordered (X); calls and types that break a `where` condition are refused where they were accepted, and a call that a `where`-clause variable can satisfy is accepted where it was refused (K).
- **Where a rung holds a line:** K, if one of its rows refuses a declaration of the compiler's own library; it lands the rest and reports.

Passing after the fix, `junit.sh skeptic-fix ...` over the rung's 17 tests and the new ones: 'link ... CondExtendInheritedMember  OK', 'run ... CondExtendInheritedMember (498ms) PASS', 'OK (19 tests)'.

### 4.2 `bd18b6a47`, contested: an `extends` entry is checked with its own conditions only

`TypeWellFormedChecker`'s trait and object declaration cases (`ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/scala_src/typechecker/TypeWellFormedChecker.scala:187-220`): where another entry of the clause is conditional, each entry is walked with the declaration's `where` clause and its own conditions; the members, the parameters and the rest are walked with all conditions, as the worker had them. The library's `List` (`AnyList`, `ZeroIndexed[\E\]` beside the conditional entry) needs no condition in its other entries, so the count is unchanged by reading. The same commit says so in `trait-parameters.tex` ("the entry itself and the declaration's members are checked as if the constraints were in the declaration's own \KWD{where} clause, and the other entries of its \KWD{extends} clause are checked without them"), in the Appendix I entry's Change and Effect, and in record.md's FACTS entry.

- The worker's argument: the brief asks that "Decls.scala's trait and object cases ... and TypeWellFormedChecker's trait and object declaration cases ... check the declaration with them holding", and REPORT.md section 1 says "TypeWellFormedChecker's trait and object declaration cases check the `extends` clause and the members' types with them holding ... Without the second, the condition's own `Ord[\E\]` was ill formed"; its specification text says "its \KWD{extends} clause and its members are checked as if the constraints were in the declaration's own \KWD{where} clause".
- My argument: the worker's reason needs the conditions in the conditional entry itself, which the fix keeps. P-151 says "its members are checked under the condition", and the curator's reading (`BOOT.md:30`) "while its members and overrides are checked, as Swift, Rust and Haskell check it": in each of those a condition holds in its own conformance only. Read over the whole clause, it admits `object Bad[\E\](x: E) extends { Wrap[\E\], Shows where { E extends Ord[\E\] } }`, which the base refuses, and whose instance `Bad[\Fn\]` is a `Wrap[\Fn\]`, an ill-formed type, and dies at link time (`CondOtherEntry`: 'NoSuchMethodError: ... CondOtherEntry$Fn.lt(CondOtherEntry$Fn)').
- Test: `ProjectFortress/compiler_tests/XXXCondExtendUnconditionalEntryChecker` (`compile`, 'has 1 error.', and the error at `:10:33-39`, 'Ill-formed type: Wrap[\E\] The static argument E does not satisfy the corresponding bound Ord[\E\].'). Before the edit (the head with 4.1), `junit.sh skeptic-entry-before ...`: 'Saw failure, but did not satisfy compile_err_contains', 'Saw wrong failure. compile' (the program compiled). After, `junit.sh skeptic-fix2 ...`: 'XXXCondExtendUnconditionalEntryChecker.fss:10:33-39:', 'File XXXCondExtendUnconditionalEntryChecker.fss has 1 error.', 'Saw expected failure', 'OK (20 tests)'.
- If the judge reverts it, the defect needs a row: "the compiled checker checks an unconditional `extends` entry with the conditions of a conditional entry beside it holding: `object Bad[\E\](x: E) extends { Wrap[\E\], Shows where { E extends Ord[\E\] } }` is accepted for `trait Wrap[\T extends Ord[\T\]\]`", with `CondOtherEntry`'s outputs, and changes.tex's line `:199-201` cited by REPORT.md goes back to `:198-200`.

### 4.3 Corrections

- `05c6be2e1`: `XXXCondExtendRefuseChecker.test` gains `compile_err_matches` over the two refused calls (`less` at `Lst[\Fn\]`, `sum` at `Vec[\String\]`). On the base's code, `old-fortress.sh /home/user/fortress-base18 .../tmp/old-caches-skeptic junit .../XXXCondExtendRefuseChecker.test`: 'File XXXCondExtendRefuseChecker.fss has 4 errors.', 'Saw failure, but did not satisfy compile_err_contains'. On the head: 'Saw expected failure', 'OK (1 test)'. With the second match spelled `Strung` for one run: 'Saw failure, but did not satisfy compile_err_matches', 'Tests run: 1,  Failures: 1'.
- `cfed7411b`: the Appendix I entry's Effect names the comparisons subsection's sentence for lists of floating-point numbers and the team's sketch of conditional subtyping (finding 4).

### 4.4 Record corrections, `2474a30bb`

record.md: a note for row 71 (6 errors on the head, `ZeroIndexed` at `:67` first; `ImportList` above); the row NEW-X-3 (1,069 characters, claim 292, notes 621): a generic trait whose `comprises` clause lists a type at a type `where`-clause variable and that overrides an inherited method crashes the overriding check, 'F is not in the kind env', from `TypeSchemaAnalyzer.subEDsolution` (`ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/scala_src/types/TypeSchemaAnalyzer.scala:198`) through `OverloadingChecker.scala:695`, `:722`, on the base and the head alike (`OpenGenericComprisesOrd`); home 3, reproducer none, as row 756's sibling crash; the FACTS entry's tests name `CondExtendInheritedMember`.

## 5. The suite my fixes needed

`ant testQuick` once, after the last code fix, on `bd18b6a47`: 'BUILD SUCCESSFUL', 'Total time: 4 minutes 19 seconds'; `CompilerJUTest` 'Tests run: 1257, Failures: 0, Errors: 0', `LibraryJUTest` 86, `OtherCompilerJUTest` 263, no failure (the worker's 1,254 plus my three cases), with ' link .../CondExtendInheritedMember  OK', ' run .../CondExtendInheritedMember (544ms) Passed', ' compile .../XXXCondExtendUnconditionalEntryChecker  Saw expected failure', ' compile .../XXXCondExtendRefuseChecker  Saw expected failure'. One contested fix, `bd18b6a47`. Nothing built or run for this ruling; every point below is read from the tree, the record and the skeptic's quoted results.

Decision: **stands**. `bd18b6a47` is upheld; nothing is reverted. The rung lands as the branch holds it.

## 1. The fix

`bd18b6a47`, "an extends entry is checked with its own conditions only": TypeWellFormedChecker's trait and object declaration cases walk each `extends` entry with the declaration's `where` clause and that entry's own conditions, wherever another entry is conditional. The members, parameters, `self`, and the `excludes` and `comprises` clauses are still walked with all the conditions (`ProjectFortress/src/com/sun/fortress/scala_src/typechecker/TypeWellFormedChecker.scala:192-202`, `:209-219`). The same commit changes the rung's own specification sentences to match (`Specification/basic/trait-parameters.tex:375-378`, and the Change and Effect of the Appendix I entry "Conditional extension"). It also adds the test `ProjectFortress/compiler_tests/XXXCondExtendUnconditionalEntryChecker`: compile, keyed on 'has 1 error.' and on 'Ill-formed type: Wrap[\E\]' at `:10:33-39`.

## 2. Ruling: uphold

**What the decision says.** P-151 (POSITIONS.md, **Only the `where` forms the team wrote down are built.**) puts two things under the condition: the subtyping ("is that type only where the condition holds") and the members ("its members are checked under the condition"). It does not name the declaration's other supertypes. The curator's accepted reading names the members and overrides, and it names the peers whose rule it takes: "the condition holds inside the declaration while its members and overrides are checked, as Swift, Rust and Haskell check it" (`explorations/coordinator/BOOT.md:30`). In each of those languages a condition belongs to its own conformance:

- Rust: `impl<T: Ord> Shows for Bad<T>`;
- Swift: `extension Bad: Shows where E: Ord`;
- Haskell: `instance Ord a => Shows (Bad a)`.

None of them lets a second, unconditional conformance assume the first one's bound.

**What the rung's own paragraph says.** The paragraph's first sentence, written by this rung and kept by both sides, is the rule the fix follows. The declared type "extends the entry's type exactly where the constraints hold: an instance whose static arguments satisfy them is of that type, and an instance whose static arguments do not satisfy them is not" (`Specification/basic/trait-parameters.tex:371-374`). An entry with no clause holds at every instance. Checking it as if another entry's constraints held assumes them at instances where, by that same sentence, they do not. The skeptic's `CondOtherEntry` shows the consequence (SKEPTIC.md, section 2's table, and 4.2):

- the base refuses `object Bad[\E\](x: E) extends { Wrap[\E\], Shows where { E extends Ord[\E\] } }` for `trait Wrap[\T extends Ord[\T\]\]` with 'Ill-formed type: Wrap[\E\]';
- the worker's head compiles it, and the run prints 'REACHED' and then 'NoSuchMethodError: ... CondOtherEntry$Fn.lt(CondOtherEntry$Fn)'.

So the worker's head accepts a program the base refuses, and that program fails at link time. `Bad[\Fn\]` is a `Wrap[\Fn\]`, a type with no meaning.

**What the team's syntax says.** The grammar attaches each `where` clause to one entry, not to the clause as a whole: *TraitTypeWhere* ::= *TraitType* *Where*? (`Specification/basic/traits.tex:83`), the node `TraitTypeWhere(BaseType baseType, Option<WhereClause> whereClause)` in the checker's AST (`ProjectFortress/astgen/Fortress.ast:1694-1697`). The team's sketch of conditional subtyping gives each entry its own condition, with unconditional entries beside conditional ones. `CommutativeMonoid[...]` carries no clause, between `Field[...] where {...}` and `TotalOrderOperators[...] where { NOT nan }` (`Specification-1.0-frozen/appendices/internal-document.tex:484-495`). One entry's condition leaking into its neighbour is not what that layout says.

**Where the worker was right.**

- The conditional entry itself has to be checked under its own condition. Without that, the condition's own `Ord[\E\]` is ill formed (REPORT.md section 1, `:22`; the base's run in its section 2, 'Ill-formed type: Ord[\E\]'). The fix keeps this: the entry is walked with `withExtendsConditions(where, List(tw))` (`TypeWellFormedChecker.scala:198-201`, `:215-218`). The worker's stated reason is met in full.
- The worker ported the probe faithfully. B.3 says "the extends clause is checked with the condition holding" (`explorations/perf-probes/where-clauses/REPORT.md:343`), and the probe's diff walks `extendsC` under all conditions.

**Where the worker was wrong.**

- The probe was a shadow measurement, not a decision. None of its tests has an unconditional entry beside a conditional one, so nothing in it tested this point.
- The brief's line for these cases, "check the declaration with them holding", places the edit (`:193`, `:203`). It does not rule on the other entries. The rung's own summary in the same brief says "its members checked with them holding". Where a paraphrase and the decision it paraphrases differ, the decision binds (POSITIONS.md, **The specification stays the standard.**).

**The skeptic's claims.**

- Right: the defect is real and is a regression from the base (above).
- Right: the fix keeps everything the worker's reason needs.
- Right: the library is unaffected. `List`'s other entries need no condition: `AnyList` takes no static parameter (`Library/List.fsi:55`), and `ZeroIndexed[\E\]` is unbounded (`Library/FortressLibrary.fsi:1330`). The same holds of `PureList`'s `List` (`Library/PureList.fss:41`). So the count does not move, by reading.
- Right: the implementation is sound. When no other entry is conditional, each entry keeps the analyzer `inDecl` (`TypeWellFormedChecker.scala:197`, `:214`), which holds that entry's conditions only. Where another entry is conditional, an entry with no clause gets `oldAnalyzer.extend(sparams, where)`, the base's analyzer.
- The suite after the fix is quoted in SKEPTIC.md section 5: `ant testQuick`, 'Tests run: 1257, Failures: 0, Errors: 0', and ' compile .../XXXCondExtendUnconditionalEntryChecker  Saw expected failure'.

**Precedent.** None in the tree. The team's checker never read an entry's clause (`TypeHierarchyChecker.scala` at `a874948ac`, "TODO: Extend to handle non-empty where clauses.", REPORT.md section 3). The judgement follows the decision on record and the peers it names.

## 3. Notes for the gather, not rulings

- REPORT.md's provenance line for the missing decision record cites `Specification/appendices/changes.tex:198-200`. After `bd18b6a47` added one line, the pointer to REPORT.md is at `:199-201`. The skeptic says so (SKEPTIC.md, section 1).
- REPORT.md section 1 still says "check the `extends` clause and the members' types with them holding". This ruling and SKEPTIC.md section 6 give the landed reading. The specification and record.md's FACTS entry already state it.
- Observed by reading only, not run and not ruled: the `comprises` and `excludes` clauses are still walked with every entry's conditions holding (`TypeWellFormedChecker.scala:201`). A `comprises` entry that is well formed only under a conditional entry's condition would be accepted in the same way. No library declaration has that shape.

\subsection{Conditional extension}
\seclabel{revival-conditional}

\begin{description}
\item[Affected section] \secref{where-clauses}.
\item[Change] A paragraph and an example are added, with a box: where the
\KWD{where} clause of an entry of an \KWD{extends} clause introduces no
\KWD{where}-clause variable and all its constraints are trait constraints,
the declared trait or object extends the entry's type exactly where the
constraints hold, and within the declaration the constraints hold while the
entry itself and the declaration's members are checked, and not while the
other entries of its \KWD{extends} clause are; the example is
\library's list, totally ordered exactly where its elements are.
\item[Rationale] This change does not follow from route~A; the revival
decided on 16~October 2026 to build the forms of \KWD{where} clause the team
wrote down, among them that a trait that extends another under a
\KWD{where} condition is that type only where the condition holds and that
its members are checked under the condition, as Haskell checks an
instance's context, Rust a conditional implementation and Swift a
conditional conformance.
The grammar gives each entry of an \KWD{extends} clause its own optional
\KWD{where} clause, and the text orders lists ``whose elements support these
same comparison operators''
(\nolinkurl{Specification-1.0-frozen/basic/operators/opr-overview.tex},
lines 284--285), which no
unconditional declaration of the list type can state:
\library\ declared their list type as lexicographically ordered at every
element type, so the compiled type checker refused the comparison of two
elements of an unbounded type in the order's own body.
The team's internal notes foresaw conditional subtyping and its cost,
that ``we may also not be able to tell whether a trait has a particular
method'' (\nolinkurl{Specification-1.0-frozen/appendices/internal-document.tex},
lines 538--543, in its subsection ``No Wrapped Fields Whose Types Are Naked
Type Variables'').
A clause that introduces a \KWD{where}-clause variable, or whose
constraints are not all trait constraints, keeps the reading it had: the
entry is extended at every instance.
\library's list keeps an element-wise \EXP{=} of its own outside the
condition, so that a list whose elements are not ordered, a list of pairs
among them, is still compared element by element.
The alternative not taken is to read the clause as limiting nothing, the
extension holding at every instance, under which the clause has no effect
and the list's order needs another construct.
The full reasoning is in
\nolinkurl{explorations/compile-ladder/rung-checker-conditional-extension/REPORT.md}
in the revival's repository.
\item[Effect] The compiled type checker reads such a clause as this
section says: a value of an instance whose static arguments satisfy the
constraints is of the entry's type, one whose static arguments do not is
refused where that type is expected, and the entry and the declaration's
members are checked with the constraints holding, its other entries without
them.
\library's \TYP{LexicographicOrder} bounds its element type by
\TYP{StandardTotalOrder}, and its list extends it under the constraint
that its element type does, so the compiled type checker orders a list
exactly where its elements are totally ordered.
It gives no order to a list of partially ordered elements, of \TYP{RR64},
\TYP{QQ} or ranges among them, where \secref{partial-total-orders} says
that a lexicographic order ``may be partial or total depending on whether the
ordering of the elements is partial or total''
(\nolinkurl{Specification-1.0-frozen/advanced-lib/algebraic-constraints.tex},
lines 520--522), and where the operators chapter's subsection
``Comparisons Operators'' compares lists ``whose elements support these same
comparison operators'', as floating-point numbers do: no partial
lexicographic order of lists is declared.
The compiled type checker still lets a member that it checked with the
constraints holding be called where they fail: it accepts a call of such
a member on an instance whose static arguments do not satisfy them
(row~NEW-X-1 of the revival's gap ledger).
Its other readers of an \KWD{extends} clause, the members a type inherits
and its checks of the type hierarchy, read the entry as extended at every
instance.
An entry under a clause that introduces a \KWD{where}-clause variable or
holds a constraint that is not a trait constraint, as the entries of the
team's sketch of conditional subtyping do
(\nolinkurl{Specification-1.0-frozen/appendices/internal-document.tex},
lines 483--512, its subsection ``Conditional Subtyping''), is read as
extended at every instance on both paths.
The interpreter reads the extension as holding at every instance, and so
does the compiled run time: a type test of an instance whose static
arguments fail the constraints answers \VAR{true} on both
(row~NEW-X-2, gated for the interpreter by
\nolinkurl{ProjectFortress/tests/XXXConditionalExtensionTypeTestWalk.fss}),
so the interpreter keeps the order of a list of tuples or of floating-point
numbers.
The code generator compiles a declaration whose \KWD{extends} clause has
such a clause; it refuses one that carries a \KWD{where} clause of its own
(row~701).
\item[Original text] No such paragraph. The grammar is unchanged:
\nolinkurl{Specification-1.0-frozen/basic/traits.tex}, line 83,
\begin{quote}
\emph{TraitTypeWhere} ::= \emph{TraitType} \emph{Where}?
\end{quote}
and the front matter lists ``where clauses and conditional extension''
among the features not yet supported
(\nolinkurl{Specification-1.0-frozen/fortress/preamble.tex}, line 82).
\item[Route C] The same under route~C.
\end{description}

# The base build, seeded worktrees and the old code

**seeding**
: Making a worktree with a copy of the build and caches of a built, clean worktree. `seed-worktree.sh` makes the copy and rewrites the paths in it (`SKILL.md`, "The caches").

**base build**
: Clean worktree at the base, built in place by ant, or seeded. Every other worktree is seeded from it.

**old code**
: Base's code, run from the base build with a private caches folder.

Once the base build is built, run its code only as "Running the old code" says, with a private caches folder outside it. Any other run writes into the caches that every worktree is seeded from.

## Finding or building a base build

- If your brief names a base build, use it.
- If not, look in `git worktree list`. Earlier base builds are at paths such as `/home/user/fortress-base<N>`. A worktree can be your base build if it passes three checks:
  - `git -C <it> rev-parse HEAD` prints your base;
  - `git -C <it> status --porcelain` prints nothing;
  - it holds `default_repository/caches/bytecode_cache/fortress.CompilerBuiltin.jar`.
- If no worktree passes them, build one at a path of your own, outside the main tree. It takes about 200 s: start the build and the library order detached, with the `nohup` line of `session.md`, "Long commands". `<base-commit>` is your base: the commit that your brief names, else your tree's `HEAD` when you start. Say so in your report.

      git worktree add --detach <base-build> <base-commit>
      cd <base-build>          # then set up the call as build-and-caches.md says
      ant compileAll
      # then the library order (build-and-caches.md), then this walk run, which warms walk's caches:
      bin/fortress ProjectFortress/tests/BooleanOps.fss
      git status --porcelain   # must print nothing: the seeding script refuses a base build that is not clean

If you check a fix against its old code, use a base build at the commit that the fix starts from. If a brief names the fix's base, the fix starts there. If not, the fix starts from `git merge-base <its branch> main`, or from the parent of its first commit on `main`.

## Seeding a worktree

A build, and a run of `bin/fortress` without a private caches folder, walk's too, write into the caches of the tree that they run in. So build and run only in a tree whose caches no other agent uses. Your brief says where you work. If your work builds or runs code and your brief gives you no tree of your own, seed a worktree of your own instead of building one. Then work only there.

Seeding takes about 3 s and 206 MB of disk. The new worktree runs walk and the compiled path right away, with the library already compiled.

    explorations/coordinator/tools/seed-worktree.sh <base-build> <new-worktree> <branch> [<start-point>]

- The script checks out `<branch>`: a local branch, else origin's, else a new branch cut from `<start-point>`, by default the base build's commit. With `-`, it makes a detached worktree at `<start-point>`.
- If the script exits 2, the base build is not built or not clean, and the script made nothing. Then make the worktree with `git worktree add`, build it yourself, and say so in your report.
- If the worktree already exists, the script keeps its branch. If it already has a build, the script keeps that too. `SEED_FORCE=1` replaces it.
- If you start in a worktree that has no build, seed it in place: name it as `<new-worktree>`, and its branch as `<branch>`.
- The script lists the library sources that differ from the base build's commit. Before a compiled run, take for each the step that `build-and-caches.md`, "After an edit of the library", gives.
- If the script warns that the copied build is the base's, run `ant compileAll`, then the library order. Without the warning, `ant compileAll` keeps the seeded caches.
- If another agent seeded your worktree, make the script's two lists yourself: `git diff --name-only <base> -- Library ProjectFortress/LibraryBuiltin` for the library sources, and `git diff --name-only <base> -- ProjectFortress/src ProjectFortress/astgen build.xml` for the warning.
- Reuse another tree's build or caches only through this script.

## Running the old code

If your worktree holds an edit and you need the base's behaviour, run the old code instead of reverting your edit. For example, see a test fail, or compare a program's old and new output.

`old-fortress.sh` runs the base build's `bin/fortress`. It sets `FORTRESS_HOME` to the base build and `FORTRESS_CACHES` to the private caches folder that you name, over your settings. Name a folder inside your worktree's `tmp/`:

    OLD=explorations/coordinator/tools/old-fortress.sh
    $OLD <base-build> <worktree>/tmp/old-caches compile P.fss     # the compiled path ...
    $OLD <base-build> <worktree>/tmp/old-caches run P             # ... then the run
    $OLD <base-build> <worktree>/tmp/old-caches P.fss             # walk
    $OLD <base-build> <worktree>/tmp/old-caches junit <worktree>/ProjectFortress/compiler_tests/X.test [Y.test ...]   # compiled .test files, in one JVM

- Any copy of the tool works, because it runs the base build that its first argument names.
- On first use, it fills the private folder with a copy of the base build's caches (36 MB, 0.04 s). Later runs use the same folder.
- Every cache file that a run writes goes to the private folder, and nothing else that it writes under the base build stays. So several agents can run the old code at once.
- Keep your programs outside the base build too, because a program writes its own logs beside it. The tool refuses a private folder inside the base build (exit 2).

To run interpreter tests on the old code, run the base build's `harness-one.sh` with `FORTRESS_HOME` set to the base build:

    FORTRESS_HOME=<base-build> <base-build>/explorations/compile-ladder/rung-inference-walk/harness-one.sh \
        <worktree>/tmp/old-harness <worktree>/ProjectFortress/tests/X.fss

The `run` step of a compiled `.test` is a separate `bin/fortress run` process. It inherits `FORTRESS_HOME` and `FORTRESS_CACHES`, and takes its class path from `FORTRESS_CACHES`. If you compose a harness run by hand with `-Dfortress.caches=<folder>`, set `FORTRESS_CACHES` to the same folder. Otherwise the `run` step fails with "Could not load ... Resource not found".

== explorations/fortress-gap-ledger.md:7-27

## The row template

A row is one line of eight cells, `| # | claim | status | class | spec citation | reproducer | found by | notes / workaround |`, at most 1,200 characters, in the table of its topic section, in number order. A pipe inside a cell is written `\|`. (POSITIONS, "The gap ledger's form"; the proposal behind it is `explorations/coordinator/process-engineering/gap-ledger-archaeology.md`, section 4.)

- **#**: the row's number, the next free one when it is added; never reused, renumbered or given to another row. 148 is vacant.
- **claim**: at most 300 characters, whose first 150 name the defect or the capability: what fails or what holds, and where.
- **status**: exactly one word of seven, with no second status and nothing in brackets:
  - `POSITIVE-VERIFIED`: it works; it ran and its output is recorded.
  - `NEGATIVE-VERIFIED`: the specification settles it and the reproducer confirms it. A row with one half fixed stays `NEGATIVE-VERIFIED`, and its notes say which half is fixed.
  - `NEGATIVE-BOUNDED`: the failure reproduces; the mechanisms tried are named and are not exhaustive.
  - `CONTESTED`: unsettled; the notes say why.
  - `RETIRED`: a source's claim falsified here, kept so that it is not derived again.
  - `FIXED`: closed by a landed commit (`ledger.py close`): the claim's first sentence, the test as reproducer, notes `fixed HASH; full text: history, row N`.
  - `DUPLICATE`: a pointer (`ledger.py duplicate`), notes `duplicate of row M; full text: history, row N`.
- **class**: `kind (area)`; `—` only for `POSITIVE-VERIFIED` and `RETIRED`. The kind is one of `implementation gap`, `library gap vs spec`, `library bug`, `design limit`, `deliberate`, `typesetter`, `packaging`; the area one of `parser`, `walk`, `checker`, `codegen`, `runtime`, `library`, `prelude`, `specification`, `tests`, `tools`.
- **spec citation**: the `.tex` file and the section heading in quotes, as `basic/operators/juxtameaning.tex`, "Juxtaposition"; a line number only against `Specification-1.0-frozen/`; `silent` where the specification does not say.
- **reproducer**: one test (its name, or its path under the test folders; an `XXX` test while it is an expected failure) or one probe path from the repository root, at most 200 characters; `none` when nothing in the tree reproduces it, with the command and its output, or the probe's old path, in the notes.
- **found by**: the stream that found it (`climb batch 8 rung I`, `run-c3`, `apl rung 2`), at most 60 characters; no date and no role.
- **notes / workaround**: at most 700 characters: `siblings: N, M` first if there are any; the mechanism, with file:line and the commit it was true at; the workaround; for a closed row, `fixed HASH`.

A path under `explorations/` that is no longer in the tree is read from history: `git show $(git log -1 --diff-filter=D --format=%h -- PATH)^:PATH`.

3. `check-index.sh`, run, and an INDEX line added for each note that it reports.
4. `PLAN.md`, its first section.
5. `BOOT.md`, the boot note, then `HELD.md`, the held list.
6. `git log --oneline -15`.
7. If the boot note says that a batch runs: the skill's `references/batch.md`, and what its "While it runs" names.

How the record is kept (FACTS, POSITIONS, their history files, INDEX and the gap ledger) is the skill's record part, `references/record.md`.

#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""The gap ledger's tool: it owns the ledger's format, reads its rows, and is
the only way to write them.

The ledger, explorations/fortress-gap-ledger.md, is sorted into topic sections,
each a "## TITLE" heading over one table of rows. A row is one line of eight
cells, and keeps its number wherever it sits:

  | # | claim | status | class | spec citation | reproducer | found by | notes / workaround |

The template (POSITIONS.md, "The gap ledger's form"; the proposal behind it is
explorations/coordinator/process-engineering/gap-ledger-archaeology.md, 4.1):
  status       exactly one of POSITIVE-VERIFIED, NEGATIVE-VERIFIED,
               NEGATIVE-BOUNDED, CONTESTED, RETIRED, FIXED, DUPLICATE
  class        `kind (area)`, kind one of the legend's seven, area one of ten;
               `—` only for POSITIVE-VERIFIED and RETIRED
  spec         the .tex file and the section heading in quotes; a line number
               only against Specification-1.0-frozen/; `silent` where the
               specification does not say
  reproducer   one test (a name under the test folders, or a path) or probe
               path from the repository root, or `none`
  limits       row 1,200 characters, claim 300, reproducer 200, found by 60,
               notes 700
  a pipe inside a cell is written \\|

Cells are split only at a pipe that is not escaped as \\|. A row whose cells
hold bare pipes (the ledger had six) does not split into its table's width that
way; it is read by its split at pipes followed by a space or the line's end, as
facts-extract.py has always read it, and check reports it under `pipe`.

Every write takes a lock (flock on .ledger.lock beside the ledger), checks the
template on the line it writes, and puts the full earlier line of a row it
changes, unchanged, in the history file beside the ledger
(fortress-gap-ledger-history.md), under "### Row N" and a line saying what
became of it. A failed check prints the rules the row breaks and exits 1.

usage: ledger.py COMMAND [ARGS] [--root DIR] [--ledger FILE] [--history FILE]

  heads                      one tab-separated line per row: number, status,
                             class, the claim's first 150 characters, and the
                             paths the row cites in backticks
  sections                   each section that holds a row table: its row
                             count and title, tab-separated
  section TITLE              the heads of that section's rows
  show N [--short]           row N under its section and table header; with
                             --short, its status, class, claim and the notes'
                             first 300 characters
  find WORDS [--open] [--cites FILE[:LINE]] [--all]
                             one line per row that holds every word (whole
                             words, or a word's start with a trailing *):
                             number, status, class, the claim's start; --open
                             leaves out FIXED, DUPLICATE and RETIRED; --cites
                             keeps the rows citing FILE (at LINE) and prints
                             the lines they cite; at most 10 rows unless --all
  count                      the rows by status, kind and area; nothing stored
  add FILE --section TITLE   FILE holds one row line, its # cell `?` (or the
                             seven cells after it); numbers it max + 1 and
                             inserts it in that section's table in number
                             order
  note N TEXT                appends TEXT to row N's notes

an instance whose static arguments satisfy them is of that type,
and an instance whose static arguments do not satisfy them is not.
Within the declaration the constraints hold: the entry itself and the
declaration's members are checked as if the constraints were in the
declaration's own \KWD{where} clause, and the other entries of its
\KWD{extends} clause are checked without them.
So a list is totally ordered exactly where its elements are:
%trait List[\E\] extends { ZeroIndexed[\E\],
%    LexicographicOrder[\List[\E\],E\] where { E extends StandardTotalOrder[\E\] } }
%end
\begin{Fortress}
\(\KWD{trait}\:\TYP{List}\llbracket{}E\rrbracket \KWD{extends} \{\TYP{ZeroIndexed}\llbracket{}E\rrbracket,\)\\
{\tt~~~~}\pushtabs\=\+\(    \TYP{LexicographicOrder}\llbracket\TYP{List}\llbracket{}E\rrbracket,E\rrbracket \KWD{where} \{E \KWD{extends}\:\TYP{StandardTotalOrder}\llbracket{}E\rrbracket\}\}\)\-\\\poptabs
\(\KWD{end}\)
\end{Fortress}
\revision{revival-conditional}{This paragraph and its example are new.
The Working Draft of February 2011 gave each entry of an \KWD{extends}
clause an optional \KWD{where} clause in its grammar and stated no meaning
for it, and its front matter lists conditional extension among the
features not yet supported.}

#!/bin/bash
# junit.sh <label> <dir-of-tests> <Name.test>... : the gather of climb batch N runs each .test through the
# harness in the main tree (fortress junit, the compiled test harness, as climb batch 6.5's gather ran its pair),
# in the order given, so that a link test runs before its XXX run test. Each named component's cache entries are
# removed before the list and after it. First line: the machine line (protocol.md, principle 2).
# ONE_JVM=1 (added 2026-09-29 for the repair on the merged tree, coordinator/climb-batch-workflow.md, "A repair
# of tests and records only"): the whole list in one fortress junit run, one JVM, as the gate's track runs them
# together; Shell junit hands the list to FileTests.suiteFromListOfFiles (Shell.java:1086), which puts its
# compile and link tests before its run tests (FileTests.java:997-1004), so a link test still runs first.
# The environment is env.sh's, set here without sourcing it, since env.sh also removes parser directories in
# /tmp. The tree is the one this script is in. FORTRESS_THREADS=4 is the pin of build.xml's fastTrack macro,
# which runs the gate's compiled tracks. The JVMs keep their temporary files, parser directories among them,
# in the tree's tmp/.
export JAVA_HOME=/usr/lib/jvm/java-25-openjdk-amd64
export PATH="$JAVA_HOME/bin:$PATH"
export FORTRESS_HOME="$(cd "$(dirname "$0")/../../../.." && pwd)"
unset JAVA_TOOL_OPTIONS
export FORTRESS_THREADS=4
mkdir -p "$FORTRESS_HOME/tmp"
export JAVA_FLAGS="-Xmx4g -Xss64m -Djava.io.tmpdir=$FORTRESS_HOME/tmp"
FH=$FORTRESS_HOME; L=${1:?label}; D=$(cd "${2:?dir}" && pwd); shift 2
cd "$FH/ProjectFortress"
CP=$(../bin/fortress_classpath | tail -1)
echo "# junit.sh $L $(date -u +%FT%TZ); nproc $(nproc); $(grep -m1 'model name' /proc/cpuinfo | cut -d: -f2 | sed 's/^ //'); $(grep -m1 'cpu MHz' /proc/cpuinfo | cut -d: -f2 | sed 's/^ //') MHz; load at start $(cut -d' ' -f1-3 /proc/loadavg); $(java -version 2>&1 | head -1); FORTRESS_THREADS=$FORTRESS_THREADS; tree $(git -C $FH rev-parse --short HEAD)$(git -C $FH diff --quiet HEAD -- ProjectFortress Library || echo ' with the next rung applied, not yet committed'); tests from $D"
clean () { for t in "$@"; do n=$(sed -n 's/^tests=//p' "$D/$t" | head -1); [ -n "$n" ] && find ../default_repository/caches -name "*$n*" -exec rm -rf {} + 2>/dev/null; done; }
clean "$@"
if [ -n "${ONE_JVM:-}" ]; then
  files=(); for t in "$@"; do files+=("$D/$t"); done
  echo "########## [$L] fortress junit, one JVM: $*"
  java $JAVA_FLAGS -Dfile.encoding=UTF-8 -cp "$CP" com.sun.fortress.Shell junit "${files[@]}" 2>&1 | sed "s#$FH/##g" | grep -v '^\s*at ' | cut -c1-240

1457:\subsection{The traits that extend a closed trait}
1:\nolinkurl{Library/List.fsi}, line 56, in the revival's repository); the
2:revival decided on 16~October 2026 to build the forms of \KWD{where} clause the
3:team wrote down, that comment among them.
4:The full reasoning of the amendment is in
5:\nolinkurl{explorations/compile-ladder/rung-size-expressions/REPORT.md} and
6:\nolinkurl{explorations/reviews/array-fork3-judgement.md} in the revival's
7:repository.
8:\item[Effect] The compiled type checker accepts the declaration of
9:\TYP{AnyIntegral} in \library\ as written
10:(\nolinkurl{Library/FortressLibrary.fsi}, lines 433--436).
11:No example of this specification changes: \TYP{ExclusiveMolecule}, which
12:has no static parameters, is still not allowed.
13:The compiled type checker enforces the requirement on a trait with static
14:parameters over the declarations and object expressions it sees: a trait or object declared in
15:another component, below such a trait and a subtype of no listed type, is
16:not refused (row~487 of the revival's gap ledger). It compares the declarations it sees by their names: for a parameterized \VAR{T} its verdict can depend on how an extender spells its static parameters, and a trait or object that extends a trait of the same simple name in another API counts as an extender (rows~489 and~490).
17:It refuses an object expression that extends a trait with a \KWD{comprises}
18:clause, explicitly or through the traits it extends, and is a subtype of no
19:listed type, as the requirement on the trait's extenders together demands of
20:it, an object expression having neither static parameters nor a clause of its
21:own; before 3~October 2026 it read no object expression against a clause
22:(row~597).
23:The interpreter checks at load the traits and objects that explicitly extend a
24:trait with a \KWD{comprises} clause declared in the component it executes, and
25:refuses one that is neither a subtype of a listed type nor another of the
26:extenders that \secref{trait-decls} allows.
27:It does not yet check a clause declared in another component, of the program
28:or of \library\ (rows~22, 487, 551, 595 and~596), an object expression that
29:extends such a trait (row~597), or that each listed type extends \VAR{T}
30:(row~598).
31:By the amendment, the compiled type checker reads a \KWD{nat} or \KWD{int}
32:\KWD{where}-clause variable as a size, reads a listed type at every value of
33:such a variable when it checks the traits and objects that extend \VAR{T}, and
34:opens an argument as the new sentence of \secref{natparams} says, so that the
35:value of \VAR{reflect} in \library\ is accepted where an
36:\EXP{N\llbracket{}n\rrbracket} is expected; it refuses an opened size that
37:reaches a type naming another size, and gives two values opened in one call
38:two sizes, so it refuses a call that needs them equal where the interpreter
39:runs it when they are.
40:It reads a declaration whose parameter type is such a trait and a declaration
41:with a \KWD{nat} parameter whose parameter type is the listed type at it as
42:applicable to the same calls, and refuses the pair as duplicates, where the
43:interpreter runs it and calls the second; the text does not say whether the
44:opening counts for the rules of \secref{overloading-static-params}
45:(row~682 of the revival's gap ledger).
46:Since 17~October 2026 it opens a type \KWD{where}-clause variable in the same
47:way, as in the clause of \TYP{AnyList} in \library\ (row~636): an argument whose
48:type is such a trait, passed where the listed type is expected, takes the listed
49:type at a type of the value's own for that call, bounded as the variable's
50:binding bounds it and by each trait constraint of the clause on the variable
51:(\secref{where-clauses}), and known to equal only itself; before 18~October 2026
52:it did not bound that type by such a constraint, and refused a call that needs
53:the constraint's bound, a call the interpreter runs (row~771); it refuses an
54:opened type that
55:reaches a type naming another type, gives two values opened in one call two
56:types, and reads a listed type at the types below the variable's bounds, its
57:binding's and its constraints', when it checks the traits and objects that
58:extend \VAR{T}, so that it refuses an extender that the clause lists only below
59:a bound its static argument does not meet; before 18~October 2026 it read a
60:listed type at every type of the variable, whatever its bound, and took such an
61:extender (row~753).
62:It does not open a trait whose clause lists a type at a type
63:\KWD{where}-clause variable where it reaches that trait as a supertype of
64:another type, so that a value of a trait that extends it, and is not itself
65:listed, is not taken where a listed type is expected (row~752); it opens a
66:trait whose clause lists a type at a size there, as before.
67:It opens such a trait, of either kind, also where it is the result type of a
68:function type, once for all the function's results, so it takes a function
69:whose results are values of the trait where a function whose results share
70:one listed type is expected, a call the interpreter refuses (row~751).
71:The code generator does not yet compile a trait with a \KWD{where} clause or
72:read a size off an argument at a call (rows~307 and~701).
73:The interpreter binds a \KWD{nat} or \KWD{int} \KWD{where}-clause variable as a
74:size, and a type \KWD{where}-clause variable as a type that stands for every
75:type, when it loads the trait, reads a listed type at every value of either in
76:its check at load, a type whatever its bound (row~754), and binds the size
77:of an argument when it dispatches.
78:It refuses at load such a trait one of whose members has a declared type that
79:names the variable, of either kind (row~755); the compiled type checker
80:accepts that declaration, and stops with an internal error at a call, outside
81:the trait, of such a member whose type names a type \KWD{where}-clause variable
82:(row~756).

1:\subsection{Overloading with static parameters}
2:\seclabel{revival-overloading}
3:
4:\begin{description}
5:\item[Affected sections] \secref{overloading-terms};
6:\secref{functional-applicability}; \secref{dotted-method-applicability};
7:\secref{resolving-overloading}; \secref{principles-overloading};
8:\secref{overloading-static-params}; \secref{resolving-coercion}; and, in a
9:draft build, the proposed features of the appendix ``Internal Document''.
10:\item[Change] The sentence of \secref{overloading-terms} that declarations of
11:one name may not differ in their static parameters, and its echo in
12:\secref{principles-overloading}, are replaced: declarations of one name may have
13:different static parameters, or some of them static parameters and others none,
14:and a declaration with static parameters is read as one declaration whose
15:parameter type ranges over its instances.
16:Such a declaration is applicable to a call when some instance of it within its
17:bounds is, and it is compared with others on the parameter types they declare,
18:taken over all their instances; the static arguments that a call does not write
19:are inferred for the declaration it selects, after the selection
20:(\chapref{type-inference}).
21:The three sentences of \chapref{multiple-dispatch} that inferred static
22:parameters before applicability was checked and before declarations were
23:compared, and the chapter's assumption that the static variables of a call have
24:been instantiated or inferred, are rewritten to match.
25:A new section, \secref{overloading-static-params}, states for declarations with
26:static parameters the three rules of the type group's paper of 2011, the No
27:Duplicates Rule, the Meet Rule and the Return Type Rule, the last checked over
28:every instance of the less specific declaration; how two parameter types with
29:static parameters exclude each other, by existential reduction with
30:instantiation exclusion; and a pair that the Return Type Rule refuses, in the
31:shape of that paper's own example, beside the pair that repairs it.
32:A box in that section states the restriction that the compiled implementation
33:adds, that of two declarations with as many static parameters of their own, one
34:of which is more specific than the other, the two agree on their static
35:parameters position by position, with an override that reorders them as its
36:example.
37:A later revision states the section's No Duplicates Rule on the relation without
38:``and not the other way round'', that $d_1$ and $d_2$ are not each applicable to
39:every call to which the other is applicable, with a box, and the box on Jan's
40:example in the internal document gives that rule as its reason.
41:A further revision has that box say that the factory of \library\ gives a
42:\TYP{Vector} where its type argument is one of the eight number types and a
43:plain array where it is any other type, \TYP{Number} among them: the factory
44:called the vector factory at its own type argument, which has no bound, an
45:instance that the bound of a \TYP{Vector}'s element type refuses
46:(\secref{type-param}), and it now builds the vector at each number type, so
47:that a \TYP{Vector} of \TYP{Number}, which is not well-formed, is no longer its
48:result.
49:\secref{resolving-coercion} says in three places that a declaration with static
50:parameters is applicable when some instance of it is, that it is compared on the
51:parameter types it declares, and that the declaration selected is then
52:instantiated, the coercions of its instance inserted statically.
53:In the internal document, the proposed features on relaxing the restrictions on
54:the static parameters of overloaded functionals and on overloading with static
55:parameters are marked done, Jan's example answered by \library's factory and the
56:questions on exclusion by the existential reduction.
57:\item[Rationale] This change does not follow from route~A; the revival decided
58:on 26~September 2026 that the sentence goes and that this working draft states
59:the model of the type group's paper of 2011 (Allen, Hilburn, Kilpatrick,
60:Luchangco, Ryu, Chase, and Steele, ``Type Checking Modular Multiple Dispatch
61:with Parametric Polymorphism and Multiple Inheritance'', OOPSLA 2011;
62:\nolinkurl{Papers/Types/rules.tick}, lines 132--180, and
63:\nolinkurl{Papers/Types/setup.tick}, lines 393--397, in the revival's
64:repository), which the compiled type checker applies, with two changes to the
65:checker: the Return Type Rule checked over every instance, and the positional
66:restriction.
67:On 28~September 2026 it decided that a coercion makes a call possible and never
68:changes which declaration runs when one is applicable without it, declarations
69:being chosen on the parameter types they declare and the declaration chosen
70:being then instantiated.
71:Neither implementation enforced the sentence: the interpreter has overloaded
72:declarations with different static parameters since May 2007, the compiled type
73:checker applies the rules of that paper to them, and \library\ overload across
74:different static parameters throughout.
75:The sentence is text of 2009.

1:using ``their bounds as their supertypes'', in a section whose type relations
2:``may be replaced when the static type checker and the type inference engine
3:are implemented'' (\nolinkurl{Specification-1.0-frozen/fortress.1.0.pdf},
4:Section~15.6.1), and the team's unfinished restart of this specification in
5:2012 dropped the sentence
6:(\nolinkurl{Documentation/Specification/Prose/Language/overloading.tick},
7:lines 100--114, in the revival's repository).
8:The restart's Types chapter (Luchangco, 2012) gives function types that hold
9:generic and plain declarations together, as sets of arrow types and universal
10:arrow types, and drops from a quantified type a static parameter that appears
11:in none of its types
12:(\nolinkurl{Documentation/Specification/Prose/Language/types.tick}, lines
13:553--558, 764--767 and 794--801).
14:The positional restriction is the compiled implementation's and not the
15:language's: its code generator hands the static arguments that a call writes,
16:by position, to whichever declaration dispatch reaches (row~398 of the
17:revival's gap ledger), while the type group's paper of 2019 instantiates a
18:dispatched declaration by substitution and renames static parameters freely
19:(Park, Hong, Steele and Ryu, ``Polymorphic Symmetric Multiple Dispatch with
20:Variance'', POPL 2019, Sections~4 and~5.2).
21:That paper's soundness proof excludes an upper bound that names a type
22:parameter, its own included, and closed types, so that \library's families over a type parameter
23:bounded by an instance of a trait at itself, such as \STR{SUM}, \STR{BIG~MAX}
24:and those over \TYP{Integral}, rest on the rules of 2011 as the compiled type
25:checker implements them, and not on the proof of 2019.
26:The full reasoning is in
